blurb: How AI is speeding up science: predicting protein shapes, forecasting weather, discovering maths and designing medicines.

steps.p: Proteins do most jobs in your body — digesting food, fighting germs, carrying oxygen. Each is a chain of building blocks called amino acids.
The chain folds itself into a precise 3D shape, and the shape decides what it does — and where a drug could attach.
steps.analogy: Like a key: the exact shape decides which lock it opens.

steps.p: Working out one shape in a lab could take months or years of X-ray experiments. Predicting it from the chain was a 50-year-old puzzle.
In 2020 DeepMind's AlphaFold 2 predicted shapes about as accurately as lab experiments, in minutes, winning the CASP competition.
DeepMind and EMBL published predicted shapes for over 200 million proteins — nearly every one known to science — free to all.

cards.q: Why does a protein's 3D shape matter so much?
options: It decides what the protein does and how drugs can attach to it
cards.why: Shape = function. Knowing the shape tells scientists how a protein works and where a medicine might fit.

cards.statement: The AlphaFold database contains predicted shapes for over 200 million proteins.
cards.why: True. Before AlphaFold, labs had measured around 200,000 shapes in decades of work.

cards.q: CASP, where AlphaFold made its name, is…
options: A two-yearly blind competition to predict protein shapes before they're published
cards.why: A blind test. Teams predict shapes that labs have measured but not yet released, so nobody can cheat.

cards.title: AlphaFold 3 (2024) predicts how proteins interact with DNA, RNA and drug-like molecules — not just their own shape.
cards.detail: Interactions are what matter for drug discovery. It uses a diffusion approach — like image generators — to build the joint structure.

cards.statement: AlphaFold explains step by step how a protein folds over time.
cards.why: False. It predicts the final shape, not the folding process. How folding happens is still studied separately.

cards.title: Learning the weather from the past

steps.p: Forecasts simulate the physics of the atmosphere — wind, heat, moisture — step by step on supercomputers for hours.
steps.analogy: Working out where a ball will land using the laws of motion.

steps.p: AI models learn from decades of past weather records how today's weather tends to turn into tomorrow's — no physics equations written in.
steps.analogy: An old sailor who's watched the sky for 40 years and just knows what's coming.

steps.p: Google DeepMind's GraphCast makes a 10-day global forecast in under a minute on one chip.

right.title: AI model
points: Under a minute on one chip

steps.p: GenCast, which gives a range of likely outcomes, beat Europe's leading forecast on 97% of tested measures.
DeepMind's GNoME predicted hundreds of thousands of new stable crystals — candidates for batteries and solar panels — though how many are truly useful is debated.

cards.q: GraphCast produces a 10-day global weather forecast in…
options: Under a minute on a single chip
cards.why: Under a minute. Training took a lot of computing, but once trained, each forecast is cheap.

cards.statement: AI weather models are trained on decades of past weather data.
cards.why: True. Mainly ERA5, a reconstruction of global weather from 1940 onward, made by combining old observations with physics models.

options: Simulating the physics of the atmosphere forward in time
cards.hint: The ball and the laws of motion.
cards.why: Simulating physics. Powerful but slow. AI models now complement it — and still rely on it to produce their training data.

cards.q: GenCast beat Europe's leading forecast on about what share of tested measures?
cards.why: About 97%. It forecasts a range of possibilities, which is especially valuable for extreme events like storms.

cards.title: Some scientists challenged how many of GNoME's predicted materials were truly new and useful.
cards.detail: DeepMind reported 2.2 million new crystals, about 380,000 predicted stable. A 2024 critique argued many were minor variations of known materials.

steps.p: A language model proposes lots of candidate solutions — often as small programs — and an automatic checker scores each one.
The best ideas are fed back to be mutated and improved, like breeding better plants over generations.
This found new solutions to open maths puzzles (FunSearch, 2023) and a faster way to multiply some matrices (AlphaEvolve, 2025).
Lean is a language where every step of a proof is checked mechanically. A made-up step simply fails.
steps.analogy: Like a spell-checker for logic — nothing wrong gets past it.

steps.p: AlphaGeometry solved 25 of 30 olympiad geometry problems in 2024, close to an average gold medallist.

cards.q: AlphaEvolve found a way to multiply two 4×4 complex-number matrices using how many multiplications?
cards.why: 48. The best known method since 1969 (Strassen's) needed 49. Saving one sounds small, but it beat a 56-year-old record.

cards.statement: Lean is a programming language and proof assistant that checks maths proofs mechanically.
cards.why: True. If Lean accepts a proof, every step is valid — no trust in the author needed.

cards.q: FunSearch discovered new maths by combining a language model with…
options: An automatic checker that scored candidate programs
cards.hint: Look at the flow in step 1.
cards.why: An automatic checker. The model is creative but unreliable; the checker keeps only what actually works.

cards.title: DeepMind's AlphaGeometry solved 25 of 30 olympiad geometry problems — close to an average gold medallist.
cards.detail: Published in 2024, it paired a language model suggesting helpful constructions with a precise reasoning engine that derived results rigorously.

cards.q: Why is computer-checked proof valuable for AI-generated maths?
options: Every step is checked automatically, so a made-up step can't slip through
It removes the need for maths
cards.why: No hallucinated steps. AI can be confidently wrong; a proof checker catches it every time.

steps.p: There are more possible drug-like molecules than stars in the universe. AI can screen huge numbers on a computer before anyone makes one in a lab.
In 2020 an MIT model screened thousands of molecules and found halicin, which killed many drug-resistant bacteria in lab tests.
David Baker's lab designs proteins never seen in nature, with shapes chosen for a job — work that won a 2024 Nobel Prize.
AI speeds up early discovery, but most time and cost is in testing on people, which can take a decade.

visual.caption: Rough time to bring a new drug to market.

steps.p: Biological data is scarce and noisy, and bodies are complicated. A molecule that looks perfect on screen can fail in people.
steps.analogy: A car that tests perfectly in a wind tunnel can still struggle on real roads.

cards.q: The antibiotic halicin, reported in 2020, was discovered by…
options: A deep-learning model screening molecules at MIT
cards.why: An AI screen at MIT. The model learned what makes molecules kill bacteria, then searched libraries for unusual candidates.

cards.statement: No drug discovered with AI has yet reached human clinical trials.
cards.why: False. Dozens of AI-discovered drugs have entered trials, some reaching late stages. None had a clear AI-only breakthrough approval by 2025.

cards.q: Why hasn't AI dramatically shortened drug development overall yet?
options: Most time and cost is in trials on people, and biological data is scarce and noisy
cards.why: Trials dominate. AI speeds up finding candidates, but proving safety and benefit in people still takes years.

cards.title: David Baker shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for designing entirely new proteins on computers.
cards.detail: His lab's tools create proteins with shapes not found in nature. One of its designs became part of an approved COVID-19 vaccine in South Korea.

cards.title: Look up a protein
cards.body: The AlphaFold Protein Structure Database is free and lets you spin 3D models of proteins in your browser.
cards.challenge: Search the AlphaFold database for "insulin" or "haemoglobin" and rotate its 3D shape.
